_(vi)_ \(|V_O^{X+Y}(H_1)|=|V_O^{X-Y}(H_1)|\) _and_ \(|V_E^{X+Y}(H_1)|=|V_E^{X-Y}(H_1)|\).

Our aim in this chapter is to cover most of the vertices of _H_ by a matching leaving only a small subset \(L^*\subseteq I_{n^{10-5}}\) uncovered. Recall that an additional property required of _L_<sup>∗</sup> is that \(|V_O^{X+Y}(L^*)|=|V_O^{X-Y}(L^*)|\) and \(|V_E^{X+Y}(L^*)|=|V_E^{X-Y}(L^*)|\). As discussed in Section 3.5, this condition is affected by use of wrap- around edges, and only affected when _n_ is odd. Hence, an additional constraint on the matching we find in _H_ is that the number of wrap-around edges using odd- even parity matches the number using even-odd parity in parts _X+Y_ and _X-Y_ . Having reached _H_ which does satisfy these parity requirements, as the process to reach _L_<sup>∗</sup> only removes disjoint matchings we only need to keep an eye on the parity conditions when _n_ is odd.

As described in Section 3.1 we plan to obtain the required matching for _H_ over a sequence of nested subgraphs \(H\supseteq H_0\supseteq H_1\supseteq\dots\supseteq H_{c_h}\supseteq L^*\), where \(H_i\subseteq I_{t_i}\). This process involves \(\Theta(\mathrm{log}(n))\) subgraphs to reach _L_<sup>∗</sup>. It is natural to think that one might try to have a larger distance between vertices of the largest index in consecutive nested intervals, however the factor 1_/c_<sub>vor</sub>∼0.8 needs to be sufficiently large to ensure the process works. In particular, the process to go from _H<sub>i</sub>_ to _H_<sub>_i_+1</sub> requires one to find a matching to cover all vertices in _V(H<sub>i</sub>_)\\_I_<sub>_t<sub>i</sub>_+1</sub>. We do this in two steps: firstly we find an ‘almost-cover’, that is, we find a matching that covers all but a _o_(1) proportion of the vertices which are present in _V(H<sub>i</sub>_)\\_I_<sub>_t<sub>i</sub>_+1</sub>. Then we run a random greedy algorithm to cover the vertices which still remain uncovered in _V(H<sub>i</sub>_)\\_I_<sub>_t<sub>i</sub>_+1</sub> after the almost-cover. To enable the random greedy algorithm to run, we need that every vertex remaining in _V(H<sub>i</sub>_)\\_I_<sub>_t<sub>i</sub>_+1</sub> is in many edges that otherwise contain only vertices in _H<sub>i</sub>_\[_I_<sub>_t<sub>i</sub>_+1</sub>\]. Since every edge that contains a vertex of index |_t_| must also contain a distinct vertex with index of order at least |_t/_2|, we certainly don’t want \(c_\mathrm{vor}\le 1/2\). Additionally, the ‘shape’ of the sets _I<sub>t<sub>i</sub></sub>_ is important to ensure that each vertex in _V(H<sub>i</sub>_) is in enough edges to ensure the random greedy algorithm does not abort. There is some flexibility to be had in both the shape of _I<sub>t<sub>i</sub></sub>_ and the value of _c_<sub>vor</sub> which ensure that the following arguments still work, but of the other possibilities, there is nothing to be gained by using a different choice.

**6.1.1. The weight shuffle.** Recall at the end of Section 3.1 we discuss the required _weight shuffle_, a process that shifts weight between edges preserving the weighted degree at each vertex. As part of the process to obtain the vortex \(H\supseteq H_0\supseteq H_1\supseteq\dots\supseteq H_{c_h}\supseteq L^*\), we obtain the almost-cover for _V(H<sub>i</sub>_)\\_I_<sub>_t<sub>i</sub>_+1</sub> using

<tbc>a _random matching tool_ (see Section 6.1.3 for details), which uses a weighting _w<sub>i</sub>_ for _H<sub>i</sub>_, such that _w<sub>i</sub>_ is an almost-perfect fractional matching for _H<sub>i</sub>_. As part of the strategy, we obtain the almost-perfect fractional matching _w_<sub>_i_+1</sub> from _w<sub>i</sub>_ for every \(i\neq 1\). The weight shuffle intervenes in this process once we have (_H_<sub>1</sub>_,w_<sub>1</sub>) and turns the almost-perfect fractional matching _w_<sub>1</sub> for _H_<sub>1</sub> into another almost- perfect fractional matching _w_<sub>1∗</sub> by transferring weight between edges via zero-sum configurations of specific forms as described in detail in Section 3.3.2. The intention of the weight shuffle is to shift weight around in such a way that the vertices closer to the centre of T do not get used too early on in the process. In particular, as we obtain disjoint edges to cover vertices remaining in _I<sub>t<sub>i</sub></sub>_\\_I_<sub>_t<sub>i</sub>_+1</sub> for each subgraph _H<sub>i</sub>_, if we use too many vertices from _I<sub>t<sub>j</sub></sub>_ where \(j\gg i\), then by the time we reach _I<sub>t<sub>j</sub></sub>_ we may have that _H<sub>j</sub>_ is too sparse to cover vertices in _I<sub>t<sub>j</sub></sub>_\\_I_<sub>_t<sub>j</sub>_+1</sub> by disjoint edges, and in this case the process would fail. The weight shuffle helps to avoid this as follows. It ensures that in our new weighting, _w_<sub>1∗</sub>, every bad edge _e_ satisfies _w_<sub>1∗</sub>(_e_)=0. This means that when covering vertices in an outer interval, we can never remove vertices too close to the centre of T at the same time. We start by ensuring that all of the weight on _c<sub>g</sub>_-bad edges is shifted to edges of type \((\alpha,\beta,0)_{c_g}\) and \((0,\beta,\gamma)_{c_g}\). We define _w_<sub>1</sub>=_w_<sub>(1_,c<sub>g</sub>_)</sub> and let _w_<sub>(1_,i_)</sub> denote the current weighting on _H_<sub>1</sub> once the reweighting of _j_-bad edges for all _j\>i_ has taken place. We shall use _i_-legal zero-sum configurations to reduce the weight on the _i_-bad edges to 0 by transferring the weight to the edges with the opposite sign in such configurations. By definition of an _i_-legal zero-sum configuration, this will subsequently shift weight from, in addition to _i_-bad edges, edges of type (0,1,3)_<sub>i</sub>_, and shift the weight onto edges of type \((\alpha,\beta,0)_i\) where \(\alpha\neq 0\), (0,0,4)_<sub>i</sub>_ and (0,1,3)_<sub>i</sub>_. Then with the updated weighting _w_<sub>(1_,i_-1)</sub>, we repeat the process to reduce the weight on all (_i_-1)-bad edges to 0, and continue until every edge _e_ in _H_<sub>1</sub> for which there exists _l_ such that _e_ contains one vertex in _K<sub>l</sub>_ and another in _I_<sub>_t_<sub>1</sub></sub>\\_K_<sub>_l_-1</sub> has _w_<sub>1∗</sub>(_e_)=0, and additionally, any edge _e_ with a vertex inside _K_<sub>1</sub> and a vertex outside _J_<sub>1</sub> also has _w_<sub>1∗</sub>(_e_)=0. The details of the running of this process follow in Section 6.2.

**6.1.2. Organisation.** In Section 6.1.3, we present the key tool that we use to do the ‘almost-cover’ at each step of the iterative matching process, a tool developed from a result of Ehard, Glock, Joos \[**18**\] which enables us at each step _i_, when we have reached _H<sub>i</sub>_, to remove a matching covering most of the vertices remaining in _I<sub>t<sub>i</sub></sub>_\\_I_<sub>_t<sub>i</sub>_+1</sub> in such a way as to ensure that the remaining graph has ‘nice’ random-like properties. In Section 6.2 we describe the process to reach _w_<sub>1∗</sub> and properties of _w_<sub>1∗</sub> given (_H_<sub>1</sub>_,w_<sub>1</sub>) as in Theorem 6.1. In Section 6.3 we describe the details of how we shall use the random matching tool in our setting and introduce new notions of reachability and graph permissibility. In Section 6.4 we give details that show a general step of the process to get from (_H<sub>i</sub>,w<sub>i</sub>_) to (_H_<sub>_i_+1</sub>_,w_<sub>_i_+1</sub>) for some \(i\in[c_h]\) and show that the process can continue to reach _L_<sup>∗</sup>. Finally, in Section 6.5, we show that a process very similar to that described in Section 6.4, but adjusted for additional parity constraints, allows us to go from _H_ to (_H_<sub>1</sub>_,w_<sub>1</sub>) as in Theorem 6.1.

<tbc>**6.1.3. The random matching tool.** One of the key tools used in our iterative absorption strategy is a generalisation of a result by Ehard, Glock and Joos \[18\] which enables us to find a matching with random-like properties given an _r_- uniform hypergraph with particular conditions. This generalises a result of Kahn \[29\] who proved a similar result, but with more restrictive conditions on properties that could be tracked in relation to the matching.

6.1.3.1. _Weighted version._ For our purposes, we wish to consider a weighted _r_- uniform hypergraph (_H,w_), where \(w:E(H)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), and \(d_w(v):=\sum_{e\unknown v}w(e)\le 1\) for every \(v\in V(H)\) (so _w_ is also a fractional matching). We write \(\Delta_w(H):=\mathrm{max}_{v\in V(H)}d_w(v)\) and letting \(d_w(v,u):=\sum_{e\supseteq\{v,u\}}w(e)\), we also write \(\Delta_w^\mathrm{co}(H):=\mathrm{max}_{\{v,u\}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(H)}{2}}d_w(v,u)\). Let \(\delta_w(H):=\mathrm{min}_{v\in V(H)}d_w(v)\).

Given a function \(p_l:\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(H)}{l}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), and a set \(\bar{v}_k\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(H)}{k}\), define

\(p_l(\bar{v}_k):=\sum_{\bar{v}\supseteq\bar{v}_k:\bar{v}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(H)}{l}}p_l(\bar{v})=\sum_{\bar{v}_{l-k}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(H)}{l-k}}p_l(\bar{v}_k\cup\bar{v}_{l-k})\)

for every \(k\le l\). Furthermore, for \(M\subseteq E(H)\), we define \(p_l(M):=\sum_{\bar{v}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(M)}{l}}p_l(\bar{v})\). Also for a function \(q:E(H)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) we define \(q(M)=\sum_{e\in M}q(e)\). Our key tool is the following:

Theorem 6.2. _Suppose_ \(\eta\in(0,1)\) _and_ \(r,L\in\mathbb{N}\) _with_ \(r\ge 2\)_. Let_ \(\epsilon:=\frac{\eta}{50L^2r^2}\) _and_ \(\psi:=\frac{\eta}{6L^2r}\)_. Then there exists_ \(\Delta_0\) _such that for all_ \(\Delta\ge\Delta_0\)_, the following holds. Let_ (_H,w_) _be an r-uniform weighted hypergraph with_ \(w(e)\ge\Delta^{-1}\) _for every_ \(e\in H\), \(\delta_w(H)\ge\frac{\Delta^{-\psi}}{1-\Delta^{-1}}\) _and_ \(\Delta_w^\mathrm{co}(H)\le\Delta^{-\eta}\) _as well as_ \(e(H)\le\mathrm{exp}(\Delta^{\epsilon^2/4})\).

_Suppose that for each_ \(l\in[L]\)_, we are given a set_ P_<sub>l</sub> of l-tuple weight functions on V(H_) _of size polynomial in_ \(\Delta\) _such that_

(6.1) \(\mathrm{max}_{v\in V(H)}p_l(\{v\})\le f\Delta^{-2\eta}\sum_{\bar{v}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(H)}{l}}p_l(\bar{v})\)

_for all_ \(p_l\in\mathcal{P}_l\)_, where_ \(f\le\frac{1}{2r!}\).

_Suppose further that_ Q _is a set of weight functions on E(H_) _of size polynomial in_ \(\Delta\) _such that_

(6.2) \(q(E(H))\ge\frac{\Delta^{1+\eta}}{1-\Delta^{-1}}\mathrm{max}_{e\in E(H)}q(e)\)

_for all_ \(q\in\mathcal{Q}\).

_Then there exists a matching M in H such that_

\(p_l(M)=(1\pm\Delta^{-\epsilon})\sum_{\bar{v}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(H)}{l}}p_l(\bar{v})\prod_{v\in\bar{v}}d_w(v)\)

_for every_ \(l\in[L]\)_, and every_ \(p_l\in\mathcal{P}_l\)_, and_

\(q(M)=\big(1\pm\Delta^{-\epsilon}\big)\sum_{e\in E(H)}q(e)w(e)\)

_for all_ \(q\in\mathcal{Q}\).

We shall show in Section 6.3 that all properties we wish to keep track of (those relating to vertex subsets, degrees and zero-sum configurations) for the general iterative absorption strategy can be written as linear combinations of functions of vertices which will satisfy (6.1). Additionally, in Section 6.5, we show that a

<tbc>particular edge related parity requirement satisfies (6.2), where it is required to proceed with one of the two initial steps of the iterative matching process.

6.1.3.2. _Deriving Theorem 6.2._ We state the theorem of Ehard, Glock and Joos \[**18**\], which is for functions on collections of edges in an unweighted graph, and then give a corollary in terms of a weighted _r_-graph. We then derive a version that is stated in terms of functions on collections of vertices, and finally derive Theorem 6.2.

In what follows, we write \(\Delta(H)\) for the maximum vertex degree of a graph _H_, and \(\Delta^\mathrm{co}(H)\) for the maximum pair degree. For \(\bar{e}_l\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{E(H)}{l}\) consisting of _l_ distinct edges from _E(H_) we say that \(\bar{e}_l\) is a _clean l_-set if the edges in \(\bar{e}_l\) are pairwise disjoint. We write \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{E(H)}{l}'\) for the set of clean _l_-sets of edges in _H_, and for \(A\subset E(H)\) we denote \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{E(H)\backslash A}{k}'\) to be the set of clean _k_-sets \(\bar{e}_k\) of edges in _E(H_) such that for every \(e\in\bar{e}_k\), we have \(e\cap a=\emptyset\) for every \(a\in A\). That is, \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{E(H)\backslash A}{k}'\) denotes the set of clean _k_-sets such that every edge in a _k_-set is disjoint from \(\bigcup_{a\in A}a\). In the theorem that follows, the properties that we consider are functions of clean _l_-sets of edges of the form \(q:\genfrac(){pt}{2}{E(H)}{l}'\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\).

Theorem 6.3 (\[**18**\]). _Suppose_ \(\delta\in(0,1)\) _and_ \(r,L\in\mathbb{N}\) _with_ \(r\ge 2\)_, and let_ \(\epsilon:=\delta/50L^2r^2\)_. Then there exists_ \(\Delta_0\) _such that for all_ \(\Delta\ge\Delta_0\)_, the following holds. Let H be an r-uniform hypergraph with_ \(\Delta(H)\le\Delta\) _and_ \(\Delta^\mathrm{co}(H)\le\Delta^{1-\delta}\) _as well as_ \(e(H)\le\mathrm{exp}(\Delta^{\epsilon^2})\)_. Suppose that for each_ \(l\in[L]\) _we are given a set_ Q_<sub>l</sub> of clean l-set weight functions on E(H_) _of size at most_ \(\mathrm{exp}(\Delta^{\epsilon^2})\) _such that_

(6.3) \(q(E(H))\ge\Delta^{k+\delta}\mathrm{max}_{T\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{E(H)}{k}^\prime}\sum_{S\supseteq T}q(S)\)

_for all_ \(q\in\mathcal{Q}_l\) _and_ \(k\in[l]\).

_Then there exists a matching M in H such that_

\(q(M)=\left(1\pm\frac{\Delta^{-\epsilon}}{2}\right)q(E(H))/\Delta^l\)

_for all_ \(l\in[L]\) _and_ \(q\in\mathcal{Q}_l\).

This theorem shows that we can find matchings in hypergraphs that act similarly to how we would expect things to look if we had picked a set of edges by choosing each edge independently with the same probability \(1/\Delta\). Whilst this result and Theorem 6.2 describe the existence of a single (deterministic) matching satisfying the conclusion for a suitably small collection of functions _p_ and _q_, this is obtained by proving the existence of a distribution on matchings for which each statement holds with high probability, and taking a union bound suffices to show that such a matching exists for which all hold simultaneously. We use this fact throughout the proof, sometimes implicitly moving between the distribution on matchings for which a statement holds with high probability and a fixed matching which satisfies many statements simultaneously. We now derive an equivalent version for weighted _r_-graphs.

Corollary 6.4. _Suppose_ \(\delta\in(0,1)\) _and_ \(r,L\in\mathbb{N}\) _with_ \(r\ge 2\)_, and let_ \(\epsilon:=\frac{\delta}{50L^2r^2}\)_. Then there exists_ \(\Delta_0\) _such that for all_ \(\Delta\ge\Delta_0\)_, the following holds: Let_ (_H,w_) _be an r-uniform weighted hypergraph with_ \(w(e)\ge\Delta^{-1}\) _and_ \(\Delta_w^\mathrm{co}(H)\le\Delta^{-\delta}\) _as well as_ \(e(H)\le\mathrm{exp}(\Delta^{\epsilon^2/4})\).

_Let q be a weight function on E(H_) _such that_ (6.4) \(q(E(H))\ge\frac{\Delta^{1+\delta}}{1-\Delta^{-1}}max_{e\in E(H)}q(e).\) _Then there is a distribution on matchings M in H such that with high probability_ \(q(M)=\big(1\pm\Delta^{-\epsilon}\big)\sum_{e\in E(H)}q(e)w(e).\) Proof. From (_H,w_) we define an unweighted multigraph \(H'\) where \(V(H')=V(H)\) and every edge \(e\in E(H)\) appears in \(E(H')\) with multiplicity \(\lfloor Dw(e)\rfloor\), where \(D=\Delta^2\). First note that \(Dw(e)\ge\Delta\), and so \(\lfloor Dw(e)\rfloor=(1\pm\Delta^{-1})Dw(e)\). In addition \(\Delta(H')=max_{v\in V(H)}\sum_{e\unknown v}\lfloor Dw(e)\rfloor\le D\), and \(\Delta^\text{co}(H')=max_{\{u,v\}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(H)}{2}}\sum_{e\supseteq\{u,v\}}\lfloor Dw(e)\rfloor\le D\cdot\Delta^{-\delta}=D^{1-\frac{\delta}{2}}.\) Finally \(e(H')\le De(H)\le Dexp(\Delta^{\epsilon^2/4})\le exp(D^{\epsilon^2/4})\). Now we define weight function \(q':H'\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) on the multigraph \(H'\) via \(q'(e)=q(e)\) for every \(e\in H'\). Note first that \(max_{e\in E(H)}q(e)=max_{e\in E(H^\prime)}q'(e)\) and also that given \(q(E(H))\ge\frac{\Delta^{1+\delta}}{1-\Delta^{-1}}max_{e\in E(H)}q(e)\), we have that \(q'(E(H'))=\sum_{e\in E(H^\prime)}q'(e)=\sum_{e\in E(H)}q(e)\lfloor Dw(e)\rfloor\)
\(=(1\pm\Delta^{-1})\sum_{e\in E(H)}q(e)Dw(e)\)
\(\ge(1-\Delta^{-1})\sum_{e\in E(H)}q(e)D/\Delta\)
\(=(1-\Delta^{-1})\Delta\sum_{e\in E(H)}q(e)\)
\(\ge\Delta^{2+\delta} max_{e\in H}q(e)=D^{1+\delta/2}max_{e\in H^\prime} q'(e)\) It follows from Theorem 6.3 with parameters \(\delta'=\delta/2,r,L\), and assuming \(\Delta\) sufficiently large, that there exists a matching _M_ in \(H'\) such that \(q'(M)=(1\pm\frac{D^{-\epsilon/2}}{2})\sum_{e\in H^\prime}\frac{q'(e)}{D}.\) Furthermore, _M_ is a matching in (_H,w_) and, by construction, \(\sum_{e\in H^\prime}\frac{q'(e)}{D}=\sum_{e\in H}\frac{q(e)}{D}\lfloor Dw(e)\rfloor=(1\pm\Delta^{-1})\sum_{e\in H}q(e)w(e).\) Hence \(q(M)=(1\pm\Delta^{-\epsilon})\sum_{e\in H}q(e)w(e),\) as claimed. □ Of course, we could have derived a weighted version that applies to all clean _l_-set weight functions, however we only require the weighted edge version for one specific application which relates only to individual edges, rather than to sets of edges. (This application comes up in the initial steps of the iterative matching

<tbc>process where parity constraints are still an issue - see Section 6.5.5.) For most of the iterative matching process the properties we are concerned with tracking are those of vertices rather than edges. As such we now derive a vertex version of Theorem 6.3. In what follows, by abuse of notation, for \(\bar{e}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{E(H)}{l}'\), and \(\bar{v}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(H)}{l}\), we write \(\bar{v}\in\bar{e}\) to mean that \(\bar{v}\) is an _l_-set containing exactly one vertex from each edge in \(\bar{e}\).

Proposition 6.5. _Suppose that H is an r-graph and_ \(p_l:\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(H)}{l}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) _is a weight function on l-sets of vertices such that_

(6.5) \(\mathrm{max}_{v\in V(H)}p_l(\{v\})\le f\Delta^{-2\eta}\sum_{\bar{v}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(H)}{l}}p_l(\bar{v})\)

_for some fixed_ \(l\in\mathbb{N}\) _and_ \(f=f(r,l)\le\frac{1}{2r^l}\)_. Then,_

(6.6) \(\mathrm{max}_{\bar{v}_k\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(H)}{k}}p_l(\bar{v}_k)\le f\Delta^{-2\eta}\sum_{\bar{v}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(H)}{l}}p_l(\bar{v})\)

_for every_ \(k\in[l]\).

This leads us to a vertex version of Theorem 6.3.

Theorem 6.6. _Suppose_ \(\eta\in(0,1)\) _and_ \(r,L\in\mathbb{N}\) _with_ \(r\ge 2\)_, and let_ \(\epsilon:=\frac{\eta}{50L^2r^2}\) _and_ \(\psi:=\frac{\eta}{5L^2r}\)_. Then there exists_ \(\Delta_0\) _such that for all_ \(\Delta\ge\Delta_0\)_, the following holds. Let H be an r-uniform hypergraph with_ \(\Delta(H)\le\Delta\), \(\delta(H)\ge\Delta^{1-\psi}\) _and_ \(\Delta^\mathrm{co}(H)\le\Delta^{1-\eta}\) _as well as_ \(e(H)\le\mathrm{exp}(\Delta^{\epsilon^2})\)_. Suppose that for some_ \(l\in[L]\) _we have p<sub>l</sub> an l-set weight function on V(H_) _such that_

(6.7) \(\mathrm{max}_{v\in V(H)}p_l(\{v\})\le f\Delta^{-2\eta}\sum_{\bar{v}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(H)}{l}}p_l(\bar{v}),\)

_where_ \(f\le\frac{1}{2r^l}\) _is fixed._

_Then there exists a distribution on matchings M in H such that with high probability_

\(p_l(M)=\left(1\pm\frac{2\Delta^{-\epsilon}}{3}\right)\sum_{\bar{v}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{V(H)}{l}}p_l(\bar{v})\prod_{v\in\bar{v}}\frac{d_H(v)}{\Delta}.\)

Proof. We start by fixing \(l\in[L]\) and defining \(q_l:\genfrac(){pt}{2}{E(H)}{l}'\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) via

\(q_l(\bar{e})=\sum_{\bar{v}\in\bar{e}}p_l(\bar{v}).\)

Claim 6.7. _q<sub>l</sub> satisfies_ \(q_l(E(H))\ge\Delta^{k+\eta}\mathrm{max}_{\bar{e}_k\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{E(H)}{k}}q_l(\bar{e}_k)\) _for all_ \(k\in[l]\).

Proof of Claim. Fix \(\bar{e}_k\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{E(H)}{k}'\) and let \(\bar{v}_{k,1},\dots,\bar{v}_{k,r^k}\) be an enumeration of the _rk_ different \(\bar{v}_k\in\bar{e}_k\). Then \(q_l(\bar{e}_k)=\sum_{\bar{e}_{l-k}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{E(H)\backslash\bar{e}_k}{l-k}}q_l(\bar{e}_k\cup\bar{e}_{l-k})\)
\(=\sum_{\bar{e}_{l-k}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{E(H)\backslash\bar{e}_k}{l-k}}\sum_{\bar{v}\in\bar{e}_k\cup\bar{e}_{l-k}}p_l(\bar{v})\)
\(=\sum_{i\in[r^k]}\left(\sum_{\bar{e}_{l-k}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{E(H)\backslash\bar{e}_k}{l-k}}\sum_{\bar{v}_{l-k}\in\bar{e}_{l-k}}p_l(\bar{v}_{k,i}\cup\bar{v}_{l-k})\right)\)
\(\le r^kmax_{i\in[r^k]}\left(\sum_{\bar{e}_{l-k}\in\genfrac(){pt}{2}{E(H)\backslash\bar{e}_k}{l-k}}\sum_{\bar{v}_{l-k}\in\bar{e}_{l-k}}p_l(\bar{v}_{k,i}\cup\bar{v}_{l-k})\right)\)

An added complication of the process described above which motivates the definition for \(\mathcal{Z}_{i,H_1}^2\) and which prevents us from dividing the weight for each _i_-bad edge _e_ evenly among all _i_-legal zero-sum configurations (and instead leads us to use a two step process to divide up the weight) is that some _i_-legal zero-sum configurations contain more than one _i_-bad edge, and so we cannot ensure that the weight on all _i_-bad edges is simultaneously reduced to precisely 0 in a straightforward manner. One alternative would be to define _i_-legal zero-sum configurations only to include those with exactly one _i_-bad edge. The issue with this strategy is that our algorithm, as well as reducing the weight on _i_-bad edges to 0, substantially increases the weight on edges of types \((\alpha,\beta,0)_i\) with \(\alpha\neq 0\). ## 6.3. Using the random matching tool

In this section we shall describe the graphs for which we wish to use Theorem 6.2, and show that all the properties we wish to track in such a graph can be described as linear combinations of functions satisfying (6.1). We shall then see in the subsequent sections that each graph to which we wish to apply Theorem 6.2 satisfies the necessary hypotheses. For _H_ and then for each \(i\in[0,c_h]\) we wish to use Theorem 6.2 on a weighted subgraph \((H_i^o,w_i^o)\) of (_H<sub>i</sub>,w<sub>i</sub>_), in such a way as to obtain a matching \(M_i^o\), and show that \(H_i[V(H_i)\backslash V(M_i^o)]\) has ‘nice’ properties with regard to valid subsets of _V_(T), as well as degree-type and zero-sum configuration conditions. We are only required to keep track of zero-sum configurations until we reach (_H_<sub>1</sub>_,w_<sub>1</sub>), as these are only required for the weight shuffle.

### 6.3.1. Key properties as functions.

As seen in the list of properties given for (_H_<sub>1</sub>_,w_<sub>1</sub>) in Theorem 6.1, the properties we are keen to track are those relating to numbers of vertices in given subsets of _V_(T), degree-type conditions, and initially also zero-sum configurations.

In this section we describe the functions and how they will be useful, assuming that they satisfy (6.1). In the section that follows we show that, given that a graph (_H<sub>i</sub>,w<sub>i</sub>_) satisfies various properties, the functions relating to the properties we wish to track in (_H<sub>i</sub>,w<sub>i</sub>_) do indeed satisfy (6.1).

6.3.1.1. _Number of vertices and weighted functions on vertices remaining in an interval._ For a fixed (hyper)graph _G_, \(S\subseteq V(\mathcal{T})\), and for some weight function \(f:V(G)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), let \(p_S:V(G)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) be given by \(p_S(v):=f(v)\unknown_{v\in V(G[S])}\). Note that we suppress _f_ in our notation, but wherever used, _f_ will be clear from the context. Then for a matching _M_, \(p_S(M)=\sum_{v\in V(M)}p_S(v)\) yields the sum of the weights _f(v_) on vertices in _V(G_\[_S_\]) which are in _V(M_). In particular, for _f_=1 (i.e. _f(v_)=1 for every \(e\in V(G)\)), _p<sub>S</sub>(M_) counts the number of vertices in _V(G_\[_S_\]) which are in _M_. Hence, the weight _f_ on vertices remaining in _S_ after removing _V(M_) from _G_ is \(\sum_{v\in V(G[S])}f(v)-p_S(M)\) and in particular the number of vertices remaining in _S_ after removing _V(M_) from _G_ is |_V(G_\[_S_\])|-_p<sub>S</sub>(M_).

Given that _p<sub>S</sub>_ satisfies (6.1) we get from Theorem 6.2 that there exists a matching _M_ in _G_ such that

(6.11) \(p_S(M)=(1\pm\Delta^{-\epsilon})\sum_{v\in V(G)}p_S(v)d_{w,G}(v)=(1\pm\Delta^{-\epsilon})\sum_{v\in V(G[S])}f(v)d_{w,G}(v).\)

As such, our algorithm to progress through the vortex of nested subgraphs will ensure that such edges are not picked up in the matching that moves the process from _I<sub>t<sub>i</sub></sub>_ to _I_<sub>_t<sub>i</sub>_+1</sub>. This notion is more complex than just covering whether a vertex is in an edge that might be useful at a particular step of the vortex, and extends to vertices that might have degree-type properties affected by edges that can be useful at a particular step.

Definition 6.18 (Reachable vertices and edges). We say that a vertex _v_ is _i_-reachable if \(v\in H_{1*}[I_{t_i}]\) and there exist \(e,f\in H_{1*}[I_{t_i}]\) such that \(e\cap I_{t_i}\backslash I_{t_{i+1}}\neq\emptyset\), \(f\cap e\neq\emptyset\) and \(f\unknown v\). Similarly we say that an edge _f_ is _i_-reachable, if \(f\in H_{1*}[I_{t_i}]\) and there exists \(e\in H_{1*}[I_{t_i}]\) such that \(e\cap I_{t_i}\backslash I_{t_{i+1}}\neq\emptyset\) and \(f\cap e\neq\emptyset\).

That is, a vertex _v_ is _i_-reachable if and only if it is feasible that the process to go from _I<sub>t<sub>i</sub></sub>_ to _I_<sub>_t<sub>i</sub>_+1</sub> might affect the degree of _v_ and an edge _f_ is _i_-reachable if and only if matching edges assigned in the process to go from _I<sub>t<sub>i</sub></sub>_ to _I_<sub>_t<sub>i</sub>_+1</sub> might then mean that _f_ is not present in the subgraph induced on vertices remaining once the vertices of the matching are removed. In particular, a vertex _v_ is _i_-reachable if and only if _v_ is in an _i_-reachable edge. Note that if _H_<sub>1∗</sub>\[_I<sub>t<sub>i</sub></sub>_\] has depth _j_, then every vertex in _K_<sub>_j_+2</sub> is _not i_-reachable. That is, all edges sharing a vertex with a vertex in _K_<sub>_j_+2</sub> are contained in _K_<sub>_j_+1</sub>, and since _H_<sub>1∗</sub>\[_I<sub>t<sub>i</sub></sub>_\] has depth _j_, every edge containing a vertex in _I<sub>t<sub>i</sub></sub>_\\_I_<sub>_t<sub>i</sub>_+1</sub> must have a vertex in _K_<sub>_j_-1</sub>\\_K<sub>j</sub>_, and so only reaches into _K<sub>j</sub>_\\_K_<sub>_j_+1</sub>. It follows that edges that are _i_-reachable have all vertices outside _K_<sub>_j_+2</sub>.

Extending the notion of reachability further, we define _reachable sets_. We want to consider sets which might lose vertices in step _i_ of the iterative matching process. Additionally we define _open and closed i-reachable pairs_ where the motivation here is to distinguish pairs (_v,S_) where step _i_ of the iterative matching process will affect the degree-type properties of _v_ relating to _H<sub>i</sub>_ and _S_.

Definition 6.19 (Reachable sets). Given that _H_<sub>1∗</sub>\[_I<sub>t<sub>i</sub></sub>_\] has depth _j_, we say that a subset \(S\subseteq V(\mathcal{T})\) is _i-reachable_ if \(S\subseteq I_{t_i}\) is _i_-valid and \(S\subseteq K_{j-1}\backslash K_{j+1}\). We also say that (_v,S_) is a _closed i-reachable pair_ if (_v,S_) is a closed _i_-valid pair, such that _v_ is _i_-reachable, \(S\subseteq I_{t_i}\) and, if _v_ has depth _j_ or _j_+1, then \(S\cap(I_{t_i}\backslash K_{j+1})\neq\emptyset\), and if _v_ has depth _j_+2 then \(S\cap(K_j\backslash K_{j+1})\neq\emptyset\). Similarly, we say that (_v,S_) is an _open i-reachable pair_ if (_v,S_) is an open _i_-valid pair, such that _v_ is _i_-reachable, \(\bigcup E_{H_{1*}}(v,S,*,*)\subseteq I_{t_i}\) and, if _v_ has depth _j_ or _j_+1, then \((\bigcup E_{H_{1*}}(v,S,*,*))\cap(I_{t_i}\backslash K_{j+1})\neq\emptyset\), and if _v_ has depth _j_+2, then \((\bigcup E_{H_{1*}}(v,S,*,*))\cap(K_j\backslash K_{j+1})\neq\emptyset\).

\(E(G^o):=\{e\in G:e\cap(I_{t_i}\backslash I_{t_{i+1}})\neq\emptyset\}\text{and}V(G^o):=\bigcup_{e\in E(G^o)}e.\)

(Since we have one degree of freedom left to dictate _z_ and only a constant number of vertices - those in _W_ - to avoid, this is possible.) Updating _E_<sub>1</sub> to _E_<sub>2</sub> by adding _z_ removes the edges \(e,e'\) from _E_<sub>1</sub> and adds edges only using new vertices outside _W_. Thus we have |_V_<sup>∗</sup>(_E_<sub>2</sub>)|_\<|V_<sup>∗</sup>(_E_<sub>1</sub>)|. Repeating the process we eventually obtain _E_<sup>∗</sup> such that \(V^*(E^*)=\emptyset\). Then _E_<sup>∗</sup> yields \(\mathbf{1}\in\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{T}^*)\), as required. □

To see that our vector **v** with a 1 on every element in _V_(T<sup>∗</sup>)\\_W_ and 0 on every element in _W_ is in L(T) simply requires checking (i)-(iv) or (a)-(d) of Lemma 3.18. It is easy to verify (i)-(iii) and (a)-(c). We give some intermediate details of the calculations for (_iv_) and (_d_) here for transparency.

When _n_ is odd (and 3|_n_), to satisfy (iv) in Lemma 3.18 reduces, after cancelling and regrouping terms, to showing that<tbc>

\(\frac{2n^2}{3}+n+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{2n}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\sum_{i\in[3]}(a_i+b_i+c_i-d_i)\in\mathbb{Z}.\)

<tbc>Then since 3|_n_, this reduces to having

\(1+2\sum_{i\in[3]}(a_i+b_i+c_i-d_i)\in 3\mathbb{Z},\)

which is the requirement given in the proof of Theorem 1.3.

Similarly, when _n_ is even and 3|_n_, to satisfy (d) and (e) in Lemma 3.18 reduces to showing that

\(\frac{n^2}{3}+\frac{n}{2}+\frac{1}{6}+\frac{n}{12}+\frac{1}{6}\sum_{i\in[3]}(a_i+b_i+c_i-d_i)\in\mathbb{Z},\)

which is equivalent to showing that

\(2+n+2\sum_{i\in[3]}(a_i+b_i+c_i-d_i)\in 12\mathbb{Z}.\)

When _n_ is even and 3 \(\unknown n\) satisfying (d) and (e) in Lemma 3.18 reduces to showing that

\(\frac{n^2}{3}+\frac{n}{2}+\frac{1}{6}+\frac{3n}{4}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\in[3]}(a_i+b_i+c_i-d_i)\in\mathbb{Z},\)

and since in this case we have \(n^2\equiv 1\) mod 3, this is equivalent to showing that

\(2+n+2\sum_{i\in[3]}(a_i+b_i+c_i-d_i)\in 4\mathbb{Z}.\)

These conditions are all satisfied by the constraints on _a<sub>i</sub>,b<sub>i</sub>,c<sub>i</sub>,d<sub>i</sub>_ given in the proof of Theorem 1.3.

We could, of course, give explicit collections for the 12 queens taken out and chosen to attack toroidally (but not classically), but the general description above shows that there are many choices for every _n_ sufficiently large.

## 7.2. Concluding remarks

Theorem 1.2, our main result, asymptotically answers an open question of Pólya [49] from 1918, as well as settling conjectures of Rivin, Vardi and Zimmerman [50] and Luria [39]. The proof of Theorem 1.2 uses the upper bounds of Luria [39] and the lower bound is our main contribution. Recall that previously there was no known non-trivial lower bound for all \(n\equiv 1,5\) mod 6 and the best lower bound for some _n_ was due to Luria [39] using very different methods. Together with Theorem 1.3 and the upper bounds of Luria both for the toroidal and classical case, we completely settle Conjecture 1.1, but we also recall that the classical case of the conjecture has been independently settled by the recent lower bound of Luria and Simkin [40] matching our lower bound in Theorem 1.3. One difference in our results, other than the vastly different strategies, is that whilst their lower bound obtains ‘almost-toroidal’ _n_-queens configurations in the sense that there are at most _o(n_) toroidal attacks for each classical configuration, our result produces the same count for an even stronger structure where we obtain the same lower bound, but counting only those configurations where at most some constant \(C\le 12\) toroidal attacks occur for each classical configuration counted. We note that the three pairs of toroidal attacks on the _X+Y_ diagonal and three pairs of toroidal attacks on the _X-Y_ diagonal used in the proof of Theorem 1.3 is not necessarily best possible for all _n_, but does indeed work for all _n_. For example, when _n_ is even and 3 \(\unknown n\), our constructions in the proof of Theorem 1.3 work taking only _i_=1 and disregarding _i_=2,3 so that we then have only one pair attacking toroidally along the _X+Y_ diagonal and only one pair attacking toroidally along the _X-Y_ diagonal.

<tbc>We also make some remarks concerning the _n_ semi-queens problem. Whilst the toroidal semi-queens problem was settled by Eberhard, Manners and Mrazovi ́c [**17**], which also gives a lower bound for classical semi-queens when _n_ is odd, there does not seem to have been any work on considering the classical version separately, or extending the lower bound from the toroidal setting to when _n_ is even. A follow- up paper by Eberhard [**16**] considers how the result of Eberhard, Manners and Mrazovi ́c, which is more generally on additive triples of bijections than just the toroidal semi-queens problem, can be extended to more abelian groups than just those of order _n_ where _n_ is odd. Perhaps the ideas used here could also give a lower bound for \(Q'(n)\). Alternatively, adapting our methods used to prove the toroidal _n_-queens result it should be possible to prove that \(T'(n)\ge((1+o(1))\frac{n}{e^2})^n\) and Luria’s upper bound also matches this. On the one hand this in itself is not very interesting since this bound is a weaker form than that already given by Eberhard, Manners and Mrazovi ́c. On the other hand, we note that our methods should also then adapt to yield a lower bound for the classical _n_ semi-queens problem, that \(Q'(n)\ge((1+o(1))\frac{n}{e^2})^n\) for all _n_ sufficiently large. Additionally, one could obtain an upper bound for \(Q'(n)\) using a fairly straight forward application of the entropy method, as done by Luria for an upper bound on _Q(n_). However given Simkin’s [**54**] new upper and lower bounds for _Q(n_), we presume that neither bound obtained this way would be tight for \(Q'(n)\). Perhaps Simkin’s [**54**] methods for _Q(n_) could similarly further improve the accuracy of approximation for bounds for \(Q'(n)\). However, as well as determining \(Q'(n)\), it is still open as to determining a value for _Q(n_) which is as accurate as our result for _T(n_), so perhaps new ideas beyond those of Simkin’s are required to close these gaps completely.

The methods we have used are inspired by powerful and recently developed tools in probabilistic combinatorics including most notably the methods of randomised algebraic construction and iterative absorption. However, these tools cannot be directly applied to the _n_-queens problem and so new ideas were needed to find variant forms applicable in our setting, making use of the combinatorial and algebraic structure embedded in the problem. There are several generalisations of the toroidal and classical _n_-queens problem discussed in Sections 6 and 8 of the survey by Bell and Stevens [**5**], including generalisations to higher dimensions. It would be interesting to consider whether some of the methods used here would enable progress on the open problems in this area.
